planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in spring into lean, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; this intergeneric hybrid between Cistus and Halimium resents winter wet far more than winter cold.

directions: Merrist Wood Cream is a low, spreading evergreen selection of the intergeneric hybrid genus x Halimiocistus, which combines a Cistus parent with a Halimium parent and shows traits of both. Each pale creamy-yellow flower carries a bold maroon-red blotch at the base of every petal and lasts only a day, but a long, heavy succession of buds keeps the mounded, gray-green foliage covered in bloom from late spring into midsummer. Like its Cistus and Halimium relatives, it thrives on neglect in lean, gritty, fast-draining soil and full sun, and it declines quickly if given rich soil, heavy mulch, or regular summer irrigation. Grow it cascading over a low wall, along a gravel path, or massed with lavender, rosemary, and other Mediterranean-climate shrubs in a hot, dry border.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; the wild Chinese species behind the popular hybrid Edward Goucher and shares its preference for excellent drainage.

directions: Abelia schumannii is a graceful, arching, deciduous to semi-evergreen shrub native to central China, valued as one of the two parent species crossed to produce the widely planted hybrid Edward Goucher abelia. It bears small, funnel-shaped, lavender-pink to mauve flowers marked with a deeper orange-throated pattern from summer into fall, each blossom backed by the persistent pinkish sepals typical of the abelia clan that extend the color display after petals drop. Its finer, more delicate branching habit than the common glossy abelia hybrid makes it a good choice for collectors and for breeding new abelia cultivars. Established plants tolerate heat and short dry spells well but appreciate a bit more afternoon shade than hardier abelia hybrids in the hottest parts of its range.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sets well without a second tree but benefits from a nearby mandarin or tangelo for heavier cropping.

directions: Ugli fruit is a naturally occurring Jamaican tangelo, a chance hybrid between grapefruit and mandarin parentage found growing wild in a Jamaican dooryard planting in the early twentieth century and later marketed commercially under the trademark UGLI. The rough, loose, puffy, greenish-yellow rind that gives the fruit its name belies a remarkably sweet, low-acid, juicy interior with the easy-peeling, segmented character of a mandarin rather than the tighter rind of a true grapefruit. Fruit typically ripens in winter and holds reasonably well on the tree, sweetening further the longer it hangs. Grow it much like other tangelos, with a warm, sheltered, frost-free site, since it shares the cold sensitivity typical of grapefruit-mandarin hybrids.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Citrus Research and Education Center
University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; one of the most reliably disease-resistant white-flowered crabapples for a specimen or street tree planting.

directions: Snowdrift bears an exceptionally heavy spring flush of pure white flowers opening from red buds, covering the rounded canopy so thoroughly that the branches are barely visible during peak bloom. Small, orange-red fruits about a third of an inch across follow and persist into winter, holding their color and drawing flocks of cedar waxwings and other fruit-eating birds after most other food sources are gone. It is widely planted for its strong resistance to apple scab and reliable annual flowering, making it a dependable, low-maintenance choice for a front-yard specimen or street tree. Prune young trees lightly in late winter to establish a strong branch framework, since mature specimens need little further shaping.

planting.note: Plant a grafted or container-grown tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, giving it room to spread wider than it grows tall.

directions: Sargent crabapple is a true wild species from Japan, introduced to Western cultivation by Arnold Arboretum director Charles Sprague Sargent, for whom it is named, after he collected it on a plant-hunting expedition in the 1890s. Unlike most tree-form crabapples, it grows as a dense, wide-spreading, mounded shrub, usually broader than tall, making it useful where a crabapple's flowers and fruit are wanted without the scale of a full-sized tree. Fragrant white flowers open from pink-tinged buds in mid-spring, followed by abundant small, dark red fruits that persist into winter and are heavily used by birds. Its compact, shrubby habit and reliable disease resistance suit it to foundation plantings, mixed borders, or mass plantings where a lower-growing flowering and fruiting accent is needed.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; develops a broadly pyramidal form valued as much for its winter fruit display as for spring bloom.

directions: Calocarpa is a naturally occurring selection of the Zumi crabapple, a hybrid found in Japan, chosen for its especially abundant crop of small, bright red, long-persisting fruit. Fragrant white flowers open from soft pink buds in mid-spring against fine-textured, lobed foliage, followed by pea-sized fruits that ripen red in fall and typically hang on well after leaf drop, providing months of winter interest and a reliable food source for birds in the lean months. The broadly pyramidal, densely branched tree eventually grows quite large, so site it with plenty of room away from walkways where dropped fruit could become a nuisance. It is a dependable, cold-hardy choice for a specimen tree where winter fruit display is a priority.
